slides.text: Gandhi came to Chhattisgarh twice — the first time as Mohandas, the second time as a Mahatma. Between those two visits lay thirteen years of fire, sacrifice, and transformation — for the man and for the land.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Split image — young Mohandas of 1920 on the left, elder Mahatma of 1933 on the right. Thirteen years of history between them as a river of faces, marches, jail bars, spinning wheels. Series 2 begins. Warm amber tones replacing the dark ochres of Series 1.

slides.text: December 26, 1920. The Nagpur Congress passes the Non-Cooperation resolution. Gandhi's first visit to Chhattisgarh has just ended. The movement is formally launched. The thirteen years begin here.
slides.visualDescription: The Nagpur Congress session, December 1920. The Non-Cooperation resolution being passed. A hall of thousands. The beginning of thirteen years of sustained resistance that will transform India — and Chhattisgarh with it.

slides.text: 1922. Chauri Chaura. A crowd burns a police station, killing 22 officers. Gandhi withdraws the Non-Cooperation Movement. Chhattisgarh receives the withdrawal with discipline — disappointed, but holding. The movement pauses; it does not end.
slides.visualDescription: Chauri Chaura — a burning police station. Gandhi's face in anguish. Then: the news reaching Chhattisgarh. Leaders receiving it with discipline. The movement pausing, not stopping. A people who understand why Gandhi withdrew, even as they grieve the pause.

slides.text: January 1922. The Nagari-Sihawa Jungle Satyagraha. Thirty-nine tribals arrested for entering their own ancestral forest. None apologised. The forest department conceded minimum wages and stopped forced labour. A small victory, completely won.
slides.visualDescription: Tribal Satyagrahis entering the reserved forest deliberately, peacefully. British forest officers arresting them. 39 people taken, none apologising. The forest department signing the wage agreement. Victory through organised dignity in ancient forest.

slides.text: 1923. The Jhanda Satyagraha. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma arrested and sentenced to six months for hoisting the national flag. A piece of cloth carrying the weight of a nation's aspiration — treated by the British as a weapon.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma hoisting the tricolor at Jabalpur. British officers arresting him. The flag continuing to fly as he is led away. The Jhanda Satyagraha — a flag as act of defiance, imprisonment as the cost of colour.

slides.text: March 12, 1930. Gandhi and 79 companions walk toward Dandi. Two hundred miles in twenty-four days. On April 6, Gandhi makes salt on the seashore. The Salt March. Chhattisgarh hears and responds.
slides.visualDescription: The Salt March — Gandhi leading companions through Gujarat. Then the news electrifying Chhattisgarh. People gathered around newspapers, faces transforming. The march reaching them across 700 kilometres as pure energy, pure inspiration.

slides.text: In Dhamtari, Narayan Rao Meghawale made salt from soil and water using an ancient method. Karan C. Tejpal bought two grams for Rs 61. Two grams of earth and water worth a man's life savings — because of what it meant.
slides.visualDescription: Meghawale making salt at the Dhamtari pond's edge. Tejpal paying Rs 61 for two grams. The transaction as ceremony — solidarity with Dandi from 700 kilometres away. Salt as the medium of a province's declaration of resistance.

slides.text: Gandhi arrested May 5, 1930. The Jungle Satyagrahas erupted across Chhattisgarh. The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha — seventeen days of sustained non-violent resistance in Mahasamund tehsil. The movement did not wait for Gandhi to lead it.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi arrested, May 1930. Then Chhattisgarh erupting — Jungle Satyagrahis entering forests, farmers refusing taxes, the Tamora Satyagraha beginning its seventeen days. The movement proved its independence from any single leader.

slides.text: The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha — a forest watchman's false claim, a community's organised refusal, seventeen days of daily arrest, police brutality, looting of crops and cattle. Women standing before bayonets and not moving.
slides.visualDescription: Tamora village — the seventeen-day Satyagraha in full. Police lathi charges. Women in a line before bayonets. Crops looted. Amar Singh being beaten. Not one person breaking discipline. The discipline of the oppressed as the highest form of power.

slides.text: Amar Singh of Khamharmuda, being beaten, ordered to shout 'Long live the King.' He said: 'Mahatma Gandhi ki Jai.' Beaten more. His wife stepped forward. Beaten too. The couple who would not change their slogan — whatever the cost.
slides.visualDescription: Amar Singh being beaten by police. His mouth forming the words: Mahatma Gandhi ki Jai. More blows. His wife stepping forward. Beaten. Neither of them changing their words. The power of a name spoken under violence. The slogan as a form of armour.

slides.text: Dayavati of Tamora — the young Gond woman who stood before a British soldier's rifle and did not move. Her name became legend. Gandhi heard about Tamora and specifically visited it in 1933. The village became Gandhigram Tamora.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati — young, Gond, standing before the rifle with her chest forward. Not moving. The soldier hesitating. The forest behind her. This image traveling to Gandhi in 1933, becoming the reason for his visit to Tamora. A woman creating a pilgrimage site.

slides.text: 1932. Congress declared illegal. Leaders imprisoned in Raipur, Nagpur, Jabalpur, Amravati. The Raipur Conspiracy Case — Parasram Soni and BB Sur charged with making explosives. The freedom struggle containing both the charkha and harder choices.
slides.visualDescription: The 1932 crackdown — Congress illegal, leaders arrested across the region. Parasram Soni and BB Sur in the British court on explosive charges. The movement's full spectrum visible: non-violence and its edge, discipline and its breaking point.

slides.text: The Raipur Congress Bhavan — constructed 1940, inaugurated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. The Congress declared illegal yet building its house in Raipur. An institution that outlasted every attempt to kill it. Permanence as defiance.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur Congress Bhavan — solid, purposeful, standing. Sardar Patel at the inauguration, 1940. The building as proof: you cannot kill an idea by making it illegal. The organisation persisting through suppression, building its permanent home.

slides.text: August 8, 1942. 'Karo ya Maro' — Do or Die. The Quit India Movement. Chhattisgarh erupted. Leaders imprisoned. Newspapers shut. Public gatherings banned. The movement going underground — and continuing.
slides.visualDescription: August 8, 1942 — the Quit India resolution. Karo ya Maro burning across Chhattisgarh. Mass arrests. Newspapers shuttered. But in back lanes and forest clearings: the movement continuing. The underground as the new front. The fire refusing to go out.

slides.text: Through those thirteen years, Gandhi had also changed. The Salt March made him a global figure. The Poona Pact made him a moral anchor. His promise to Ambedkar — to fight untouchability for life — defined his final mission.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's transformation: the Salt March, his imprisonment, meeting Ambedkar, signing the Poona Pact. The younger Mohandas becoming the global Mahatma. Each experience adding depth to the face. The man who will return to Chhattisgarh in 1933 already visible.

slides.text: The Poona Pact, September 1932. Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerwada jail. Ambedkar and Gandhi facing each other — two giants, two visions of India's future. The agreement reached. Gandhi's promise made: untouchability for life.
slides.visualDescription: Yerwada jail, September 1932. Gandhi fasting. The tension between Gandhi and Ambedkar made visible — two powerful men, both committed to Dalit uplift, differing on method. The Poona Pact signed. Gandhi's life-promise made. A covenant that will bring him to Chhattisgarh.

slides.text: Sevagram Ashram near Wardha — Gandhi's base on the Nagpur-Mumbai rail route. From here he planned the Harijan tour. The tour that would take him across India, beginning with Chhattisgarh. The ashram as command centre of truth and non-violence.
slides.visualDescription: Sevagram Ashram — spare, simple, purposeful. Gandhi at his desk planning the Harijan tour. Maps of India. The route beginning in Chhattisgarh. The ashram as the origin point of the second visit. Simplicity as the foundation of a complex mission.

slides.text: Gandhi started a nationwide journey to prepare the public against untouchability. It was a coincidence that his journey started from Chhattisgarh — the same land where he had begun his national work in 1920. The land that received him first, received him again.
slides.visualDescription: The Harijan tour beginning — Gandhi's itinerary map showing the starting point in Chhattisgarh. A coincidence that is also a homecoming. The land that received him first as Mohandas now receives him first as The Mahatma. The symmetry of history.

slides.text: November 22, 1933. A train approaches Durg. Gandhi is accompanied by his secretary Mahadev Desai, Thakkar Bapa, Kumari Meera Ben — the Englishwoman Madelaine Slade — and Jamunalal Bajaj's daughter Madalsa Narayan.
slides.visualDescription: The train approaching Durg, November 22, 1933. Inside the compartment: Gandhi, Mahadev Desai with his notebook, Thakkar Bapa, Meera Ben — the English devotee in Indian dress — and Madalsa Narayan. A diverse group bringing a single mission.

slides.text: Thirteen years separate the two visits. In 1920, Gandhi came to support a canal Satyagraha. In 1933, Gandhi comes to fight untouchability — the deepest wound in Indian society. The second visit has a different weight, a different purpose.
slides.visualDescription: The contrast between 1920 and 1933: the Kandel canal on one side, a temple door on the other. A water tax versus a caste barrier. The first visit about land and rights; the second about human dignity at its most fundamental. Same man, deeper mission.

slides.text: In November 1933, Gandhi was engaged in the works of untouchable emancipation continuously for five days. He reached Durg on November 22, made Raipur his centre, and took several meetings till November 27.
slides.visualDescription: The itinerary of the second visit: Durg, Raipur, Dhamtari, Bilaspur, village circuits — five days, multiple cities, continuous movement. Gandhi at the centre of a wheel of purpose, moving outward to reach every community, every temple, every village.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — who brought Gandhi to Chhattisgarh in 1920 — had been working on untouchability throughout the thirteen years between visits. He had done this before Gandhi named it as his central cause. Gandhi would acknowledge this.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma through thirteen years — continuously working on untouchability. Temple entry, Janeu movements, the Satnam Ashram. Gandhi arriving in 1933 to find that Sharma has been doing this work longer than Gandhi himself has made it his mission.

slides.text: Gandhi looked at Pt. Sundarlal Sharma and said: 'Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain.' You are even my Guru in the salvation of Harijans. The student acknowledging the teacher who preceded him. Humility as the mark of the truly great.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi face to face with Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — Gandhi's hands on Sharma's shoulders, looking at him with deep respect. The words: Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain. The most powerful man in India calling this Chhattisgarhi reformer his guru.

slides.text: The five days of the second visit would take Gandhi to places that had earned the right to receive him: Durg, Raipur, Dhamtari, Bilaspur, village after village. Each stop a reckoning with untouchability — the wound that independence could not cure alone.
slides.visualDescription: The map of the second visit unfolding: Durg on November 22, Raipur at the centre, Dhamtari on the 25th, Bilaspur on the 24th, village circuits on 26-27, departure on 28. Five days drawn on the map of Chhattisgarh as lines of pilgrimage.

slides.text: Ghanshyam Singh Gupta told Gandhi about the integrated school in Durg — Baithd School at Shanichari Bazar — where since 1926, children of upper castes and Harijans had studied together on the same sackcloth. Gandhi visited. He was moved.
slides.visualDescription: The Baithd School in Durg — children of all castes sitting together on the same sackcloth since 1926. Ghanshyam Singh Gupta telling Gandhi about it. Gandhi visiting. His face as he sees what should be normal everywhere. The school as proof of what is possible.

slides.text: Gandhi also had food while sitting with the children of the untouchable class at Baithd School. Not a symbolic gesture — a meal. Together. The Mahatma eating beside children who were told they polluted the air around them. Truth made edible.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi seated on the floor of Baithd School, eating a meal alongside Harijan children. Simple sackcloth under them. The principal watching. The children eating without fear. The most radical act in India 1933 — two humans eating food together.

slides.text: He reached Durg on November 22 and made Raipur his center. A night procession from Amapara to Budhapara, Raipur — three hours to travel a short distance. Aarti at every step. Flowers and lamps lining the road.
slides.visualDescription: The night procession in Raipur — from Amapara to Budhapara. Three hours for a short road. At every step: aarti, flower petals, lit lamps on both sides. Gandhi moving through a corridor of devotion. The city refusing to let him arrive quickly.

slides.text: The crowd estimate tells the story: it took more than three hours to reach Shukla Niwas from Amapara. The city had not seen anything like this. Ravi Shankar Shukla — who received Gandhi in 1920 as DCC secretary — now received him at his own home.
slides.visualDescription: Shukla Niwas at Budhapara, Raipur — the home of Ravi Shankar Shukla. Gandhi arriving after three hours through the crowded streets. Shukla receiving him — the man who was DCC secretary in 1920, now a senior leader. Thirteen years visible in both their faces.

slides.text: Gandhi stood at the window of Shukla Niwas and greeted the crowd that would not disperse. The city had not seen anything like this devotion. The Mahatma at the window — a figure of immense consequence in a simple cotton dhoti, greeting his people.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the window of Shukla Niwas — the crowd in the street below refusing to leave. Gandhi folding his hands toward them. The city at night, lit by lamps and devotion. The Mahatma in the window as an image that Raipur will carry forever.

slides.text: The second visit has begun. Five days of purpose, of temple doors opened, of Harijan children eating beside the Mahatma, of a lakh people at Victoria Garden, of a barber receiving a rupee worth more than gold. The five days of The Mahatma.
slides.visualDescription: A preview of the second visit's moments — the Baithd School meal, the temple doors opening, Victoria Garden crowd of one lakh, Makhan the barber's moment, the village circuits. Five days compressed into one frame. The promise of what is to come.

slides.text: Thirteen years changed everything. The man changed. The land changed. The movement changed. But one thing did not change: the love that Chhattisgarh had for Gandhi, and the respect that Gandhi had for what Chhattisgarh had done in his absence.
slides.visualDescription: The unchanged love — the same emotion on Chhattisgarh's faces in 1933 that was there in 1920. Different people, same feeling. The movement aged but not diminished. Gandhi aged but not weakened. Love as the constant through thirteen years of fire.

slides.text: In the second visit, Gandhi also met the inheritors of the first visit — the children of the movement, those who had grown up under the influence of 1920 and were now adults in the movement of 1933. Generations connected by one man's two visits.
slides.visualDescription: Young adults of Chhattisgarh in 1933 — people who were children in 1920, now active participants. The generation that grew up under the influence of the first visit, now fully in the movement of the second. Thirteen years as the bridge between generations.

slides.text: The second visit was about untouchability — India's deepest wound. Gandhi had promised Ambedkar. He had promised himself. He came to Chhattisgarh first because Chhattisgarh had proven, through Pt. Sharma's decades of work, that it was ready.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi arriving in Chhattisgarh specifically because of Sharma's work — the Satnam Ashram, the Janeu movements, the integrated school. Chhattisgarh as the most prepared ground for the Harijan mission. The first province because the most ready province.

slides.text: November 22, 1933. The Mahatma is in Chhattisgarh. He will not return after this. These five days are the last time this land will see him. Every moment of the second visit is therefore the most precious — the final gift.
slides.visualDescription: November 22, 1933 — Gandhi in Chhattisgarh for the last time. The finality invisible to those welcoming him. They think he may return. He will not. These five days: the last gift of his presence to a land that gave him its best.

slides.text: The words of the book: 'Gandhi infused a political, social, and economic consciousness within the entire state. Gandhi inspired the world's great moral and political leaders — and he began that journey from here, from this land.'
slides.visualDescription: The full arc visible — from Gandhi's first inspiration in South Africa, through India, to Chhattisgarh in 1920 and 1933. The land at the center of a story that is also a world story. Chhattisgarh not peripheral but essential to what Gandhi became.

slides.text: Five days remain. November 22 to November 28, 1933. Five days in which temples will open their doors to Harijans, a lakh will gather at Victoria Garden, a barber will ask only to touch Gandhi once, and an old woman will ask to wash his feet.
slides.visualDescription: A calendar showing November 22-28, 1933. Each day marked with its defining moment. Five days laid out as a path of pilgrimage. The reader invited to walk through them. The promise of the second series made in its first episode.

slides.text: Thirteen years of fire. And now The Mahatma arrives. Next: Episode 2 — The Fire of Tamora.
slides.visualDescription: The Chhattisgarh landscape — the same forests, the same rivers, the same soil that received Gandhi in 1920. Now receiving him again. Thirteen years older, thirteen years more ready. Title card: Episode 2 — The Fire of Tamora.
